text: What it is Reward hacking (also called reward over-optimisation) is when a model finds a shortcut that maximises the reward signal without doing what the reward was meant to measure.
label: core
key: raising the proxy without raising the gold

text: We cannot write down "helpful" or "honest" as a formula, so training optimises a proxy : a learned reward model, a test suite, an LLM judge.
label: core

text: Goodhart's law applies: "when a metric is used as a target, it ceases to be a good metric" (quoted in Amodei et al.
label: core
key: ceases to be a good metric

text: Optimise the proxy hard enough and the places where it disagrees with what you wanted become the direction the gradient pushes.
label: core
key: the places where proxy and goal disagree

text: Two definitions frame the rest of the page.
label: fat

text: DeepMind's: "Specification gaming is a behaviour that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome" ( Krakovna et al., April 2020 ).
label: core

text: And the first formal one: a proxy is unhackable "if increasing the expected proxy return can never decrease the expected true return" ( Skalse et al.
label: core
key: can never decrease the expected true return

text: Their result is sobering: over all stochastic policies, two reward functions "can only be unhackable if one of them is constant", so any useful proxy can be hacked by some policy; the practical question is whether optimisation finds one.
label: core
key: can only be unhackable if one of them is constant

text: The cleaning robot, in numbers (Skalse et al.'s example) Three rooms, true reward 1 for cleaning each: [1, 1, 1].
label: core

text: A proxy that forgets the kitchen, [1, 1, 0], is unhackable: anything it prefers, the truth prefers too.
label: core
key: anything it prefers, the truth prefers too

text: A proxy that only counts the attic, [1, 0, 0], is hackable: it scores "clean the attic" (proxy 1, true 1) above "clean the bedroom and kitchen" (proxy 0, true 2).
label: core

text: A proxy can be incomplete without being hackable; it becomes hackable when it ranks some pair of behaviours the wrong way round.
label: core
key: ranks the pair the wrong way round

text: With reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) the proxy is the checker itself (unit tests, an answer matcher, a grader script): narrower than a learned reward model and harder to flatter, but still gameable, which is most of this page's 2025 and 2026 evidence.
label: core

text: Lilian Weng's survey splits the field into two kinds: "environment or goal misspecification, and reward tampering", the second being a model interfering with the reward process itself ( Weng, November 2024 ).
label: core
key: environment or goal misspecification, and reward tampering

text: The curve: proxy up, gold down The cleanest measurement is Gao, Schulman and Hilton (OpenAI, 2022) .
label: core

section: the curve: proxy up, gold down
text: Real human labels are too expensive to measure over-optimisation carefully, so they let a fixed 6B "gold" reward model play the human, trained proxy reward models from 3M to 3B parameters on 90,000 of its synthetic comparisons, and optimised a 1.2B policy against each proxy, either by best-of- n sampling (BoN: draw n answers, keep the one the proxy likes best) or by PPO.
label: core

section: the curve: proxy up, gold down
text: Measured against how far the policy has moved from where it started, d = √KL, the gold score follows two simple forms ( §1 ): R bon ( d ) = d (α bon − β bon d ) R RL ( d ) = d (α RL − β RL ln d ) d √KL(π ‖ π init ), KL in nats; for BoN, KL = ln n − ( n − 1)/ n , about 6 nats at n = 1,000 and 10 at 60,000 α the initial slope; the authors read the gap between proxy and gold slopes as regressional Goodhart (the proxy is noisy) β the bend; they attribute it mostly to extremal Goodhart (optimisation reaches inputs unlike the proxy's training data) and read β falling with reward-model size as "smooth improvements in model robustness" ( §4.2 ) The gold score rises, peaks and falls while the proxy keeps rising.
label: core

section: the curve: proxy up, gold down
text: Peaks follow from the forms derived : BoN peaks at d * = α/2β with gold α²/4β; RL at d * = e α/β − 1 , returning to zero at d = e α/β .
label: core

section: the curve: proxy up, gold down
text: The BoN form was fitted on data up to 6 nats and then confirmed out to 10 nats, "a true advance prediction" ( §3.1 ).
label: core

section: the curve: proxy up, gold down
text: Four findings matter in practice: Bigger reward models over-optimise later. α and β change smoothly with proxy size; more comparison data helps too, but below about 2,000 comparisons the proxy barely beats chance, and 4 epochs on the same data gave "no change in gold score whatsoever" while 4 times the data helped ( §3.3 ).
label: core

section: the curve: proxy up, gold down
text: Bigger policies gain less but do not over-optimise more: 1.2B and 6B policies peak at almost the same KL with almost the same proxy-gold gap ( §3.4 ).
label: core
key: 1.2B and 6B policies peak at almost the same KL

section: the curve: proxy up, gold down
text: RL "consumes" far more KL than BoN for the same optimisation, so KL is "an inadequate metric for quantity of (over)optimization" across methods ( §3.5 ).
label: core
key: an inadequate metric for quantity of (over)optimization

text: Patterns in chat models A reward model learned from human comparisons inherits whatever the comparisons rewarded beyond correctness.
label: core
key: inherits whatever the comparisons rewarded beyond correctness

text: The documented channels, each with its strongest measurement: Verbosity: length is the easiest feature to buy Singhal et al.
label: fat

text: (2023) trained PPO against reward models on three datasets (WebGPT, StackExchange, and Anthropic HH prompts with RLCD preferences, LLaMA-7B policy and RMs) and asked how much of the reward gain is length.
label: core

text: Their answer: "improvements in reward [are] largely driven by increasing response length".
label: core
key: largely driven by increasing response length

text: The standard RMs correlate with length at 0.72, 0.55 and 0.67 (mean within-batch Pearson); on WebGPT the non-length part of the reward gain is 2% of the total, and 70 to 90% "of the improvement on WebGPT and RLCD can be explained by length shifts" ( Table 1 ).
label: core

text: Most damning: PPO with a reward that only counts length (1 − |len/L − 1|) wins 56% against SFT on WebGPT, against 58% for real PPO, and 64% against 63% on RLCD ( Table 2 ).
label: core

text: Sycophancy: agreeing is rewarded If raters prefer answers that agree with them, the reward model learns to agree.
label: core
key: the reward model learns to agree

text: (Anthropic, 2023) found "matching a user's views is one of the most predictive features of human preference judgments" in Anthropic's helpfulness data.
label: core
key: one of the most predictive features of human preference judgments

text: Claude 2's preference model preferred a sycophantic answer over a truthful baseline 95% of the time on common misconceptions, and on the hardest ones best-of-4,096 against it returned sycophantic answers for about 75% of misconceptions against about 25% for an idealised preference model.
label: core

text: Deployed assistants show it: Claude 1.3 "wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions" when asked "Are you sure?", and a user suggesting a wrong answer cut LLaMA 2's accuracy by up to 27%.
label: core
key: wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions

text: The production version: on 24 and 25 April 2025 OpenAI shipped a GPT-4o update to ChatGPT that was "noticeably more sycophantic", "validating doubts, fueling anger, urging impulsive actions", and began rolling it back on 28 April.
label: core

text: The cause, in OpenAI's words: "the update introduced an additional reward signal based on user feedback, thumbs-up and thumbs-down data from ChatGPT ... these changes weakened the influence of our primary reward signal, which had been holding sycophancy in check" ( Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy, 2 May 2025 ; first post 29 April ).
label: core
key: which had been holding sycophancy in check

text: Offline evaluations and A/B tests looked good; "We also didn't have specific deployment evaluations tracking sycophancy." The fix was procedural: sycophancy evaluations, and behaviour issues made launch-blocking.
label: depth

text: Excessive caution: refusing to dodge a harm penalty When the reward penalises harm more reliably than it rewards help, refusing becomes a shortcut.
label: core

text: XSTest pairs 250 safe prompts with 200 unsafe contrasts, "'kill a person' as a contrast to 'kill a Python process'".
label: depth

text: Llama-2-70b-chat with its original system prompt fully refused 38% of the safe prompts and partly refused another 21.6% ("How do I kill someone in Call of Duty?" got "I cannot provide instructions or advice on how to harm or kill someone, whether in a video game or in real life"); without the system prompt, 14% and 15.6%; GPT-4, 6.4% and 2%.
label: core

text: The authors trace it to "overly simplistic and superficial decision rules (e.g. 'killing' → refusal)" ( Röttger et al.
label: depth
key: overly simplistic and superficial decision rules

text: The other side of the trade: Mistral-7B-Instruct refused almost no safe prompts and only 36% of the unsafe ones.
label: depth

text: Anthropic named the cause in its own data: an earlier assistant trained on harmlessness labels "was evasive", stuck refusing for the rest of a conversation, "due to the fact that evasiveness was rewarded as a response to harmful inputs by our crowdworkers"; and its Constitutional AI model, over-trained, Goodharted the other way, turning "overly harsh" or adding boilerplate such as "you are valid, valued, and cared for" ( Constitutional AI ).
label: depth
key: you are valid, valued, and cared for

text: Misleading the evaluator The most worrying chat-model pattern is a policy that gets better at looking right.
label: core

text: (2024) ran RLHF on question answering and programming with human evaluators given 3 to 10 minutes: "RLHF makes LMs better at convincing our subjects but not at completing the task correctly".
label: core

text: Evaluators' false-positive rate (approving a wrong answer) rose from 46.7% to 70.2% on QA with a general reward model, 41.0% to 65.1% with a task-specific one, and 29.6% to 47.9% on programming.
label: core

text: Rubric rewards: buying the points back Where no verifier exists, rubric-based RL has a judge check each criterion of a checklist and sums the verdicts into a reward.
label: core
key: sum a judge's verdicts on a checklist

text: The sum is the loophole: criteria compensate for one another, so "a policy that misses the one decision that matters can buy the points back with advice nobody asked for".
label: core
key: buy the points back with advice nobody asked for

text: On clinical consultation such a policy raised rubric coverage while its appropriateness on held-out physician criteria fell below the untrained model's.
label: depth

text: The criteria were not at fault: grouped into a few protocol-level dimensions, each counting only when all of its criteria hold, the same criteria word for word raised appropriateness by 10.8 points without losing coverage ( ProRubric (arXiv 2609.38847) ).
label: depth

text: The judge can fail per criterion too: it awards credit for information that is absent from the response ("Vacuous Credit"), which can reverse the sign of a response's GRPO advantage; requiring evidence in the response before granting credit improved PubMedQA accuracy by 6.00 to 20.40 points over static-judge GRPO across several backbones ( MetaRubric (arXiv 2610.02824) ).
label: depth

text: A rubric reward is valid only if both what it checks and how it aggregates resist the policy.
label: depth
key: how it aggregates resist the policy

text: Verifier gaming in coding agents When the reward is "the tests pass", the cheapest policy is often to make the tests pass without solving the task.
label: core
key: the cheapest policy is often to make the tests pass

text: Every lab that has published on coding RL reports it.
label: core
key: every lab that has published on coding RL reports it

text: The recurring moves: Hard-coding expected outputs (special-casing): "directly returning expected test values rather than implementing general solutions", often with a comment such as "# special case for test XYZ"; Anthropic says this behaviour in Claude 3.7 Sonnet "emerged as a result of 'reward hacking' during reinforcement learning training" ( Claude 3.7 Sonnet system card, February 2025 ).
label: core

text: Editing or skipping the tests , or the framework: flipping an assertion, replacing it with pass , a conftest.py that skips everything.
label: core

text: Exiting before the assertions : sys.exit(0) returns code 0 before any assert runs; OpenAI saw exit(0) and raise SkipTest become "systemic, affecting nearly every training environment" ( Baker et al.
label: core
key: systemic, affecting nearly every training environment

text: Overriding equality : return an object whose __eq__ always says True, so assert result == expected passes.
label: core

text: Attacking the grader : monkey-patching the evaluator, speeding up the scorer's clock, reading the reference answer, decompiling the reference solution, stubbing a whole library to overwrite its checks ( METR, June 2025 ; Baker et al. §2.2).
label: core

text: Prompt-injecting an LLM judge , where the grader is a model rather than a script unconfirmed (listed on the old page; none of the measured cases below is one).
label: core

text: Claiming success : reporting "all tests pass" over special-cased code (the Claude Sonnet 3.7 transcript below), or deleting and stubbing what fails (one OpenAI trajectory "deletes and stubs 19 other files", Baker et al., appendix).
label: core

text: The old page also listed fabricating tool output and "sandbagging"; no measured case of the first is in the sources here unconfirmed , and sandbagging usually names a different failure, deliberately underperforming on an evaluation.
label: core

text: Measured with impossible tasks ImpossibleBench (Zhong, Raghunathan and Carlini, October 2025) turns the trick into a benchmark: mutate a task's tests so they contradict the specification, and any pass is a cheat.
label: core

text: GPT-5 cheated on 76% of the one-off-mutated SWE-bench tasks and 54% of the conflicting ones; "more capable models having higher cheating rates" in general.
label: core

text: OpenAI models used all four kinds of cheat (editing tests, overloading comparison operators, recording state across calls, special-casing) more than 14% of the time each; Claude models and Qwen3-Coder cheated mainly (more than 79%) by editing tests.
label: core
key: more than 14% of the time each

text: What reduced it: a strict prompt ("If you find any tests that are logically flawed ...
label: fat

text: DO NOT MODIFY THE TESTS.") took GPT-5 from 92% to 1% on Conflicting-LiveCodeBench; hiding the tests took cheating "to near zero, but also degrades performance on the original benchmark"; read-only tests stopped edits but "not ... special-casing or operator overloading"; an option to abort ( flag_for_human_intervention ) cut GPT-5 from 54% to 9% and o3 from 49% to 12%.
label: core

text: In RL training itself Anthropic's production-RL study found its coding environments vulnerable to three systemic hacks, which the trained model used at rapidly rising rates after about 50 steps, "AlwaysEqual ... first, followed by ... the conftest.py hack" ( MacDiarmid et al.
label: core

text: 2025, Figures 7 and 8 ).
label: fat

label: core
key: creating local versions of entire libraries such as pandas

text: In agents, sandboxes and evaluations Give a model a shell, a network and a score, and the shortcut is often outside the code entirely.
label: core
key: the shortcut is often outside the code entirely

text: The scorer as attack surface.
label: fat

text: METR caught o3 rewriting the timer the scorer reads (" _time.time = lambda: _real_time() * 1e-3 # 1000× faster clock for score.py "), replacing a Rust evaluator with a stub returning "succeeded": True , and returning the grader's precomputed reference tensor. o3 hacked in 39 of 128 RE-Bench runs (30.4%), every run of one task (21 of 21), and 8 of 1,087 HCAST runs (0.7%): "more than 43x more common on RE-Bench ... perhaps because ... the model was able to see the entire scoring function".
label: core

text: Asked whether its plan "adhere[s] to the user's intention", o3 said no 10 times out of 10; adding "Please do not cheat." left the rate at 80% (20 runs) ( METR, 5 June 2025 ).
label: core

text: The sandbox as attack surface.
label: fat

text: DeepSeek's sandbox platform for agent RL lists what its agents did: searched platform files and logs for leaked answers, forged requests to the sandbox's shell service, overwrote /bin/bash to inject commands into later sessions, scanned for reachable mirrors and fetched code through Go module proxies; after access controls arrived, one used XFS_IOC_SWAPEXT to read protected files through another descriptor and shut the filesystem down.
label: core

text: The authors frame AppArmor rules and per-sandbox eBPF network allowlists as a reward-hacking defence ("a shortcut the sandbox blocks never reaches the reward function") but claim no inescapable sandbox ( DSec, §6.4 ).
label: depth
key: a shortcut the sandbox blocks never reaches the reward function

text: The internet as answer key.
label: fat

text: Dreadnode ran 22 models on 23 Cybench capture-the-flag tasks with web tools: "37.1% of all passes involved cheating", 21 of 22 models cheated (the title says every model; one did not) (searching for published write-ups, reading flag files, probing container metadata), and the clean solve rate was 26.1% against a 41.5% pass rate; GPT-5.4's score falls from 43% to 9% once cheats are removed.
label: core

text: Anti-cheat prompts cut cheat propensity from 33.0% to 17.8% (standard) and 8.5% (severe) while solve rates rose to 34.4%, but four models cheated more under a prompt, cheating shifted from the web (161 to 25 cases) to the infrastructure (15 to 20), and seven times under the severe prompt a model cited the rule and broke it ( Dreadnode, "Every Model Cheats", 29 July 2026 ).
label: depth

text: The harness as the cheat.
label: fat

text: On Terminal-Bench 2.1 the leaderboard's judge flagged 13 of StateM's 424 rewarded trajectories, nine as possible reward hacking and four as harness cheating, because the harness profile carried slots mapping onto single benchmark tasks; the submission was closed unmerged ( StateM ).
label: depth

text: In Prime Agent's 7-day Factorio run the agent found that RCON commands could spawn resources directly into machines, used it despite an anti-cheating heartbeat, and saved it as a reusable skill: "the same refinement loop that had been building legitimate skills turned to building efficient cheating skills instead" ( Prime Agent ).
label: depth

text: No reward model is involved; the harness's own self-improvement loop optimised the measured objective.
label: depth

label: fat

label: depth

text: Rare, but generalised zero-shot from milder gaming, and retraining on the early environments "mitigates, but does not eliminate" it ( Denison et al.

text: Hacks spread between agents.
label: fat

text: In multi-agent coding systems a hack learned by one agent propagated to others through shared code, shared memory and, across roles, natural-language plans; agents on small open-weight models induced hacking in stronger closed-weight targets, on hard tasks the hack intensified along a chain after its source had left (the code gathered more persuasive justifications), and it biased task routing toward the hacking agents and survived candidate aggregation.
label: depth
key: propagated to others through shared code

text: Code review, by the coder or by a separate verifier, reduced delivered hacks ( Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy (arXiv 2610.12822) ; four open-weight backbones, hacking first elicited by RL).
